prompt: What is a standby, in terms of earlier lessons?

choices.text: A logical dump reloaded every night
choices.why: A standby is physical: it replays the log into a copy of the files.

choices.text: A second primary that accepts writes
choices.why: A standby is read-only until it is promoted.

choices.text: A base backup that never stops recovering
choices.why: Right. It receives the log as it is written and replays it continuously.

choices.text: A snapshot taken every few seconds
choices.why: Snapshots are copies at instants; a standby replays every change.

prompt: Put the path of one change from the primary to a query on the standby in order.
hint: Four steps, four columns in pg_stat_replication.
items: The primary writes it to its own log and commits
The WAL sender sends the new log
The standby writes and flushes it to its pg_wal
The standby replays it into its data files
trap: Nothing is visible to a query on the standby until the last step; each step can lag the one before.

prompt: A `DELETE` with the wrong `WHERE` runs on the primary. What does the standby have a second later?
hint: Replication copies changes, all of them.

choices.text: The same rows lost, on both servers
choices.why: Right. Replication protects against losing a server; backups protect against losing data.

choices.text: The rows, because standbys ignore deletes
choices.why: A standby replays every change the primary logged.

choices.text: A warning and a paused replay
choices.why: Nothing in replication judges whether a change was a mistake.

choices.text: The rows, until the next checkpoint
choices.why: Checkpoints do not delay replay.

prompt: What can the role created with `LOGIN REPLICATION` do?
hint: It was given exactly one right.

choices.text: Read every table, so it can copy them
choices.why: A physical standby copies files and log, and needs no rights on tables.

choices.text: Create databases on the standby
choices.why: Nothing on a standby is created by hand; it replays the primary.

choices.text: Promote the standby
choices.why: Promotion is an administrator's act on the standby, not a right of this role.

choices.text: Receive the log, and nothing besides it
choices.why: Right. It cannot read a single table.

prompt: Why does the replication password go in `/var/lib/postgresql/.pgpass` rather than in `primary_conninfo`?
hint: What does a backup of the data directory copy?

choices.text: Because primary_conninfo cannot hold a password
choices.why: It can; that is exactly what the lesson avoids.

choices.text: Backups copy that file
choices.why: Right: a password there would sit in a file every backup copies. postgresql.auto.conf lives in the data directory, and travels with every base backup.

choices.text: Because .pgpass encrypts the password
choices.why: It is plain text, protected only by its permissions.

choices.text: Because pg_hba.conf reads it
choices.why: pg_hba.conf decides which connections are allowed; it reads no password file.

prompt: Match each `pg_basebackup` option with what it does here.
hint: Three make it a standby, one brings the log.

pairs.right: Writes the replication settings and standby.signal
Creates the replication slot on the primary
Names the slot to create and use
Brings the log written during the copy

right_distractors: Compresses the copy on the way

prompt: An empty file called `___.signal` in the data directory makes PostgreSQL start as a read-only copy that follows a primary.
hint: The kind of server it makes.

prompt: In `pg_stat_replication`, what does `sync_state: async` tell you?

choices.text: The standby is behind and catching up
choices.why: That would show in the LSN columns, not in sync_state.

choices.text: Commits do not wait for this standby
choices.why: Right: the primary does not wait for this standby to confirm a commit. Commits return as soon as the primary has them.

choices.text: The standby is not connected
choices.why: A disconnected standby has no row in the view at all.

choices.text: The standby replays faster than the primary writes
choices.why: sync_state says nothing about speed.

prompt: All four positions in `pg_stat_replication` read `0/4000000`. What does that say?

choices.text: Replication has stopped at that position
choices.why: state was streaming; nothing new had been written.

choices.text: The slot is full
choices.why: Slots do not fill; the positions agree because there was nothing to send.

choices.text: The standby has written the log but not replayed it
choices.why: replay_lsn equals the others; it has replayed it.

choices.text: It has replayed all the primary has written
choices.why: Right: the standby has everything the primary wrote, replayed. When they differ, the gaps are replication lag.

prompt: What did the standby answer to an `INSERT`?
hint: It applies the primary's history and makes none of its own.

choices.text: A read-only transaction error
choices.why: Right: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. Lesson 19 is about how applications find the server that accepts writes.

choices.text: It forwarded the INSERT to the primary
choices.why: PostgreSQL never forwards writes; the application has to send them to the primary.

choices.text: It accepted it and replicated it back
choices.why: Replication runs one way, primary to standby.

choices.text: It queued it until the next promotion
choices.why: Nothing is queued; the statement fails.

prompt: What problem does a replication slot solve?
hint: Without one, the primary recycles on its own schedule.

choices.text: Standbys reading uncommitted data
choices.why: Standbys only replay committed history; slots are about retention.

choices.text: Two standbys replaying in different orders
choices.why: Each replays the same log in the same order.

choices.text: A lagging standby finding its log already recycled
choices.why: Right: without it, a standby that falls behind finds its log recycled. The slot makes the primary keep every segment the standby still needs.

choices.text: The primary sending log too fast
choices.why: Slots do not throttle anything.

prompt: With the standby stopped and three updates run, how many MB of log did the slot hold?
A standby was decommissioned on Friday, but its slot was left on the primary. What happens by Monday?

choices.text: Nothing: an inactive slot is ignored
choices.why: An inactive slot keeps its promise with nobody to collect.

choices.text: The slot expires after 24 hours
choices.why: Slots never expire by default.

choices.text: The primary promotes the standby automatically
choices.why: Nothing promotes anything here.

choices.text: The kept log fills the primary's disk
choices.why: Right: the primary keeps the weekend's log, and its disk fills. A full disk stops the primary. Watch for inactive slots and drop them.

prompt: What did `max_slot_wal_keep_size = '32MB'` do to the inactive slot holding 49 MB?

choices.text: Deleted the slot
choices.why: The slot still exists; it is marked lost.

choices.text: Moved the log to the standby
choices.why: The standby was stopped; nothing moved.

choices.text: Marked it as lost
choices.why: Right: marked lost, so its segments can be recycled. The primary chose its own disk over the standby, which is the right choice.

choices.text: Archived the log it held
choices.why: A slot only holds log back; copying it anywhere is the archiver's job, not the limit's.

prompt: After its slot was lost, the standby was started again. What did it say, and what is the fix?
hint: requested WAL segment has already been removed.

choices.text: Log gone; rebuild from a base backup
choices.why: Right: its segment was removed, so it is rebuilt from a new base backup, unless an archive can supply the missing log.

choices.text: It caught up from the primary after a delay
choices.why: The primary no longer had the segment, so there was nothing to catch up from.

choices.text: It promoted itself, since the primary refused it
choices.why: A standby never promotes itself.

choices.text: It restarted the primary to recover the segment
choices.why: A standby has no control over the primary.

prompt: A standby must survive a four-hour network outage. The primary writes 5 GB of log an hour. What is the smallest `max_slot_wal_keep_size`, in GB?
How does an archive beside the slot change what happens when a slot is lost?
hint: Where else can a standby get old segments?

choices.text: It prevents slots from ever being lost
choices.why: The cap still applies; the archive makes losing the slot survivable.

choices.text: It fetches old segments from the archive, then streams
choices.why: Right: the standby fetches the missing segments from the archive, then streams again. The slot keeps recent log close; the archive keeps the rest. Lesson 13 builds it.

choices.text: It makes the primary keep log for longer
choices.why: The archive is a copy elsewhere; the primary's pg_wal is unchanged.

choices.text: Nothing; standbys cannot read archives
choices.why: A standby with restore_command reads the archive like any recovery.

prompt: A team has one standby, a slot with no cap, and no backups because "the standby is our backup". Which two failures are they exposed to?
hint: One from each half of the course.

choices.text: Slow queries on the standby, and a slow primary
choices.why: Performance is not what this setup risks.

choices.text: A network outage and a power cut
choices.why: The standby helps with both; those are what it is for.

choices.text: A dead standby's slot, and a replicated DELETE
choices.why: Right. An uncapped slot turns a dead standby into an outage, and nothing protects data from a bad statement.

choices.text: None, if the standby is in another building
choices.why: Distance helps with fires, not with deletes or full disks.
